The only piece of wreckage recovered from the "unsinkable" MS Hans Hedtoft, which struck an iceberg and sank on its maiden voyage, 1959

MS Hans Hedtoft was a Danish liner that struck an iceberg and sank on 30 January 1959 on her maiden voyage off the coast of Western Greenland. The only piece of wreckage ever found was a lifebelt.

Hans Hedtoft was 82.65 metres (271 ft 2 in) long, with a beam of 14.17 metres (46 ft 6 in) with a double bottom and seven watertight compartments and an armoured bow and stern. She was designed to provide a year-round service between Denmark and Greenland. Like the RMS Titanic, Hans Hedtoft was said to be the safest ship afloat, being described as "unsinkable" by some. With a crew of 40, 55 passengers and a cargo of frozen fish on board, it collided with an iceberg about 35 miles (56 km) south of Cape Farewell, the southernmost point of Greenland and sunk. No survivors or wreckage except this life ring, which was found nine months later washed up on shore, was recovered.

She was the last known ship sunk by an iceberg with casualties.

Here is what she looked like.

Hans Hedtoft was the Danish Prime Minister twice during the 1940s and 50s.
